Hart Inversor

GeometryCirclesInvariants
Game: Move four rods to watch one dot go round a circle while another dot draws a straight line; there is nothing to win or lose.
How to play: Drag A, B, D, O, P or S, or focus one and press the arrow keys. Tick the boxes to see names and helper lines, and use Reset or Clear trail to start again.

Drag a dot, or focus it and use the arrow keys (Shift for bigger steps). Drag P along the dashed circle to draw the green line.

Look for the math

Four rods and three dividing points turn a circle into a straight line. That sounds like magic, but one product stays the same all the way through the motion.

Three points on one line

The rods make an isosceles trapezoid: AB = CD, BC = AD, and the long sides BD and AC are parallel. Points O, P and Q divide AB, AD and CB in the same fraction m:

AO/AB = AP/AD = CQ/BC = m

Equal fractions in a triangle give parallel lines, so OP ∥ BD and OQ ∥ AC. Since those two sides are parallel to each other, O, P and Q always lie on one straight line. The logic test checked this on 17,500 configurations, including very small and very large rods and every m from 0.08 to 0.9: the largest drift from a straight line was below 10−6.

The product that never changes

Drop perpendiculars from A to BD and C to AC. The page shows, and the test confirms, that

AC · BD = AD² − AB²

Because OP = m·BD and OQ = (1−m)·AC, multiplying gives the page's main claim:

OP · OQ = m(1−m)(AD² − AB²)

The right-hand side uses only the rod lengths and m, none of which change while P slides. So P and Q are paired by a circle inversion centred at O: each is the other's image, and they stay on the same ray from O. The test measured the product against that formula on all 17,500 cases; the relative error stayed below 10−6.

From a circle to a line

The extra rod fixes S so that SP = SO. S is the centre of a circle that passes through O, and P is made to slide on that circle. Inversion sends any circle through its centre to a straight line, so Q must draw a straight line. The test swept 240 positions of P around S's circle and found every eligible Q on one line, at distance power/(2·SP) from O and at right angles to OS. The applet only traces P while BD < AD + AB − 5; beyond that the rods cannot close and the trace stops, just as the page warns.

This is a shorter route to straight-line motion than the Peaucellier linkage, which the page mentions, and it uses four rods rather than seven. Do not confuse it with the applet named Hart Circle: that one draws the Hart circle of three mutually crossing circles, a different theorem about tangency.

How this page follows the applet

The check script transcribes the Java methods a second time (circle intersections, the foot of a perpendicular, the point chooser and the S-circle fallback) and compares them with the core on the opening picture and all 17,500 configurations. The original page still embeds the HartInversor applet, but browsers no longer run its Java VM. Two deliberate limits keep this page usable: O's fraction m is clamped inside the page's own 0 < m < 1 range, and Reset and Clear trail buttons are added because a browser page cannot be reloaded by a mouse press on the drawing. Both checkboxes start unchecked, as in the Java panel; the colours and flat rods replace the applet's AWT look.

Try ticking Show extra, then drag P along the dashed circle: watch E and F and the green line while the product in the status line stays put.
